common_name: Folsom's Weeping Yaupon Holly (Cascading Native Holly with Heavy Berry Crops)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in late winter, spring, or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Folsom's Weeping is a female selection first found near Folsom, Louisiana, whose long pendulous branches cascade downward rather than mounding like the species.

directions: Folsom's Weeping is grown chiefly for its distinctive habit, with slender branches that drape downward in curtains rather than holding an upright or rounded form like most yaupon selections. As a female clone it sets a heavy crop of small orange-red berries each fall that hang along the drooping stems and persist well into winter, so siting a male yaupon nearby improves fruit set. It can be trained as a large weeping specimen shrub or limbed up over time into a small cascading tree, and like other yaupon selections it shrugs off heat, drought, salt spray, and periodic wet soil once established. Give it room to develop its pendulous form rather than shearing it, since heavy pruning removes the arching branch tips that give the cultivar its character.

common_name: Scarlet's Peak Yaupon Holly (Narrow Columnar Female Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun; Scarlet's Peak is a patented, densely fastigiate female yaupon selected in Mississippi as a narrower, berry-bearing counterpart to the male columnar cultivar Will Fleming.

directions: Scarlet's Peak grows as a dense, narrow exclamation-point column, staying just a few feet wide even as it reaches well over ten feet tall, which makes it useful for tight side yards, screening, or repeated vertical accents where a spreading shrub would not fit. Because it is a female selection, it needs a male yaupon such as Will Fleming or an unselected seedling within pollinating range to produce its crop of small red berries, unlike the male-only columnar cultivars grown purely for form. Its tightly held, dark green foliage requires little to no shearing to maintain the columnar silhouette, saving maintenance compared to shaping rounded hedges. As with other yaupon selections, it tolerates heat, drought, salt spray, and a wide range of soils once established, needing supplemental water only through its first year or two.

common_name: Carolina Ruby Yaupon Holly (Dwarf Compact Heavy-Fruiting Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Carolina Ruby is a patented dwarf female yaupon selection bred for an unusually heavy set of bright red berries on a compact, low-maintenance frame.

directions: Carolina Ruby combines the compact, mounding size of a dwarf yaupon with the reliable heavy berry production usually associated with taller female selections, flowering over several weeks in early spring before setting fruit. Because it is female, planting a male yaupon cultivar nearby is necessary to pollinate the flowers and achieve the bright red winter fruit display the cultivar is grown for. Its small stature suits foundation plantings, low hedges, and mass groupings where a full-size female yaupon would quickly outgrow the space. Like other yaupon selections it is highly heat- and drought-tolerant once established and needs only light shaping to keep its naturally dense form.

common_name: Baby Jewel Yaupon Holly (Rounded-Leaf Dwarf Native Holly)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Baby Jewel is a patented dwarf female yaupon distinguished from other compact yaupon cultivars by its rounded, closely whorled leaves and dense, mounding habit.

directions: Baby Jewel stands apart from other dwarf yaupon selections by its rounded rather than narrow leaves and short internodes, which whorl the dark green foliage tightly along the stems for an unusually dense, fine-textured mound. It is a female cultivar that begins setting a heavy crop of small red berries while still young and small, so even recently planted specimens can show good fruit set given a male pollinator nearby. Bred and field-tested under harsh heat and drought conditions in north Texas, it tolerates blistering summers and poor soil with minimal irrigation once roots are established. Its tight, naturally rounded form works well in foundation plantings, low borders, or containers without regular shearing.
